resources.string: Follow a mechanism step by step and explore the related structures. Views show anatomy; they do not simulate movement or disease.
These journeys use the complete male atlas, which includes the required organs. The mechanisms described are shared by both sexes. Choose this atlas to begin.

This view locates structures at organ scale. Microscopic details and processes described in the text are not depicted. Close the panel to rotate or enlarge the model; resume the journey from the menu.

Connect the path of air, the diaphragm, the lungs and blood circulation.

Air enters through the nose or mouth, then reaches the trachea and bronchi. Airways branch within the lungs down to the alveoli, where gas exchange takes place. The view shows the trachea, main bronchi and lung lobes.

During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and moves down; the chest cavity enlarges and air enters. Intercostal muscles contribute. During quiet exhalation, muscle relaxation and the elastic recoil of the lungs help air leave. The model remains still.

Oxygen crosses the alveolar wall into capillaries and is carried largely by hemoglobin in red blood cells. Carbon dioxide moves in the opposite direction before being exhaled. Alveoli, capillaries and red blood cells are not visible in this external lung view.

The right heart sends oxygen-poor blood to the lungs through the pulmonary arteries. Pulmonary veins return it to the left heart, which pumps it to the body. Artery and vein describe direction relative to the heart, rather than oxygen content.

Brain centers control breathing and receive information about blood gases. Needs change with activity: ventilation increases during exercise. Breathing and circulation cooperate to supply tissues. The view brings together the related organs without depicting this nervous control.
Understand how the heart fills, contracts and adjusts its rhythm.

Each side of the heart has an atrium and a ventricle. The right side serves the lungs; the left serves the rest of the body. Valves limit backflow. This external view shows the whole heart without a cross-section of its chambers or valves.

The signal normally starts in the sinoatrial node in the right atrium. It spreads through the atria, then slows at the atrioventricular node, allowing the ventricles to finish filling. It then activates the ventricles. This electrical system is not drawn in the model.

Ventricular contraction ejects blood; relaxation allows filling. Normal heart sounds are associated with valve closure: first the mitral and tricuspid valves, then the aortic and pulmonary valves. The model produces neither beats nor sounds.

The pulse reflects heartbeat frequency. During exercise, the heart speeds up to support oxygen delivery to muscles. The nervous system and hormones modulate its rate and strength. A pulse alone does not describe all aspects of heart function.
Follow food along the digestive tract and discover the organs that supply digestive secretions.
Chewing fragments food; saliva starts digesting starch. The tongue helps swallowing. In the esophagus, coordinated contractions called peristalsis push the food bolus toward the stomach.

The stomach mixes food with acidic and enzymatic secretions that help digest proteins. It gradually passes this mixture, called chyme, to the small intestine. Digestion combines mechanical and chemical processes.

The liver makes bile; the gallbladder stores and releases it into the small intestine. It helps digest fats. The pancreas supplies digestive enzymes. Food passes through the duodenum, rather than through these three organs.

The duodenum, jejunum and ileum form the small intestine. Digestion continues here and most nutrients are absorbed. Blood and lymph then transport them. The view shows intestinal segments without their microscopic villi.
The large intestine absorbs water; bacteria help transform residues. Stool moves to the rectum, where it is stored before elimination. Digestion also involves nervous and hormonal control.
An example of airway disease to explain the mechanism. The model shows reference anatomy; this journey provides neither a diagnosis nor treatment instructions.

Asthma is a chronic airway disease. Airways can become inflamed and narrowed, hindering airflow, especially during exhalation. The bronchi and lungs locate the problem; the model does not show these pathological changes.

Pollen, viral infections, cold air or exercise may trigger or worsen symptoms in some people with asthma. Triggers vary. Worsening symptoms may be an attack; this list is insufficient to identify the cause of breathing difficulty.

Air must reach the alveoli to renew the gases exchanged with blood. Breathing difficulty can impair these exchanges. The heart then carries blood to tissues: lungs and circulation complement each other. This view measures neither obstruction nor oxygenation.
Explore protection, movement, blood cell production and bone renewal.

The skull surrounds the brain; vertebrae protect the spinal cord. The skeleton also supports the body and provides muscle attachments. This view shows the bony enclosures without depicting the nervous tissues they protect.

Ribs and the sternum help protect the heart and lungs. The thoracic skeleton is also associated with breathing movements. Protection does not mean immobility: bones, cartilage and muscles cooperate. The view relates the rib cage to the organs it houses.

Muscles transmit forces to bones; joints allow movement between them. Bones can act as levers. In the arm, the humerus, radius, ulna and biceps illustrate this cooperation. The model locates structures without simulating their forces.

Bone stores minerals including calcium and phosphorus. Red marrow produces blood cells; yellow marrow stores lipids. These internal functions cannot be seen on the surface of the femur. Not every adult marrow cavity contains active red marrow.

Bone tissue is continually remodeled: osteoclasts resorb bone and osteoblasts form it. Mechanical stress, nutrition and hormones influence this renewal. Adult bone therefore remains biologically active; its outer shape alone does not reveal its strength.
